anchors.context: Jack choked on the rotten fumes. His eyes watered.

wave.meaning: A small movement of the hand to say hello.
wave.whyHard: Not the usual meaning! Usually a wave means a moving hill of water.

waved.meaning: Moved a hand to say hello or good-bye.
waved.whyHard: This word is less common than the school words for the same idea.

waving.whyHard: This word is less common than the school words for the same idea.

weird.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
weird.example: I heard a weird noise in the night.
weird.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

western.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
western.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

whirl.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
whirl.example: She whirled around when she heard her name.
whirl.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

whisper.meaning: To speak very quietly, using your breath.
whisper.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
whisper.example: She whispered the answer in my ear.
whisper.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wild.meaning: Not controlled; messy or going in all directions. "Wildly" means in a fast, excited way, without control.
wild.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
wild.example: The wind blew her hair wild.
wild.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

witness.meaning: To see something happen with your own eyes.
witness.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
witness.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wonder.meaning: To want to know something; to ask yourself. "I wonder where we are" means "I want to know where we are."
wonder.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
wonder.example: I wonder what time it is.
wonder.whyHard: A common word with more than one meaning. Check the meaning here.

senses.meaning: "No wonder" = it is not surprising ("No wonder I think it’s weird here").
senses.whyHard: Not the usual meaning! Usually: To want to know something; to ask yourself.

anchors.context: No wonder I think it’s weird here

wooden.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
wooden.example: There was a wooden box under the bed.
wooden.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

workmen.meaning: People whose job is building or digging.
workmen.whyHard: This word is less common than the school words for the same idea.

yay.meaning: A word you shout when you are happy.
yay.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.
yay.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yeah.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.
yeah.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yikes.meaning: A word you say when you are surprised or a little afraid.
yikes.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.
yikes.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

paragraphs.context: The idea for this Magic Tree House book was inspired by a small article
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer got the idea for this book from a newspaper article.
paragraphs.simple: The writer read a short newspaper story. It said that scientists had found an old library of scrolls in a Roman town called Herculaneum. A volcano covered that town almost 2,000 years ago. The same volcano also destroyed Pompeii.

background.note: Herculaneum was a small Roman town in the south of Italy. It was buried by the volcano Mount Vesuvius in the year 79, at the same time as Pompeii.
Pompeii was a Roman town near the sea in the south of Italy. In the year 79 the volcano Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried it under ash. Today people visit its ruins.

paragraphs.context: I have always wanted to write a book about Pompeii
paragraphs.mainIdea: She moved the library to Pompeii in her story.
paragraphs.simple: She always wanted to write about Pompeii, so she used her imagination. In her story the library is in Pompeii, and Jack and Annie must find a lost scroll just before the volcano erupts.

paragraphs.context: I hope you’ll enjoy taking this scary journey
paragraphs.mainIdea: She hopes readers will enjoy the scary trip.
paragraphs.simple: The writer hopes you will enjoy this scary adventure with Jack and Annie, as much as she enjoyed writing it.

paragraphs.context: Jack reached into his drawer and took out his secret library card.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack looks at his secret library card.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took his secret library card out of a drawer. It was a thin piece of wood with the shiny letters M L on it.

background.note: M L stands for "Master Librarian". Jack and Annie got these cards from Morgan at the end of Book 12.

paragraphs.context: Jack couldn’t believe that he and his sister, Annie, were finally Master Librarians.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is happy that they are Master Librarians now.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was surprised and happy that he and Annie were now Master Librarians.

background.note: In the series, Jack and Annie solved four riddles and became Master Librarians. Now they travel in time to save lost books.

paragraphs.context: He wondered if he should pack the secret card to take on vacation.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The family is going on vacation soon.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought about taking the card on vacation. His family would soon leave for a week in the mountains.

paragraphs.context: Just then Annie stuck her head into Jack’s room.
paragraphs.simple: At that moment Annie put her head into Jack's room and asked him to go to the woods with her.

paragraphs.context: Every morning, they looked in the Frog Creek woods
paragraphs.mainIdea: They check the woods every day for the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Every morning Jack and Annie went to the woods to see if Morgan and the magic tree house had come back.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is a magical librarian from the old stories about King Arthur. She owns the magic tree house.

paragraphs.context: “We can’t,” said Jack. “We’re leaving soon.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says no, because the family is going on a trip soon.

paragraphs.context: “But what if Morgan’s there?” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks: what if Morgan is in the tree house, waiting for them?

paragraphs.context: He grabbed his backpack. He threw in his notebook
paragraphs.simple: Jack took his backpack and put his notebook, his pencil and his secret library card in it. Then he went downstairs after Annie.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t go far!” their dad called.
paragraphs.simple: Their dad says not to go far, because the family leaves in twenty minutes. Annie says they will be back in ten.

paragraphs.context: Right, thought Jack. Five minutes to the woods
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack knows they will not be late.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought: five minutes to go to the woods, five minutes to come back. Even if they go on an adventure, they will come back at the same time they left.

background.term: return at exactly the same time
background.note: In the series, no time passes at home while Jack and Annie travel in the tree house.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran out their front door.
paragraphs.simple: They run out of the house in the bright morning sun, across the grass and down the street.

paragraphs.context: “I had a nightmare last night,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she had a bad dream last night. This is a clue to the story.

paragraphs.context: “I dreamed fires were burning,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie had a bad dream about fire.
paragraphs.simple: Annie dreamed of fires, smoke, darkness and shaking ground. She asks if the dream was a warning.
paragraphs.tone: This dream tells the reader what will happen later in the story.

paragraphs.context: “Nah,” said Jack. “Nightmares never come true.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says bad dreams never really happen.
paragraphs.tone: The reader may guess that Jack is wrong.

paragraphs.context: They left the sidewalk and headed into the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They walk to the tallest tree.
paragraphs.simple: They left the street and went into the quiet woods. They walked between trees in the sun until they came to the tallest oak.

paragraphs.context: There it was—the magic tree house.
paragraphs.simple: They see the magic tree house, and Morgan le Fay is waving from the window.

paragraphs.context: “Hail, Master Librarians,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan greets them in an old, formal way.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says hello in a very old and polite way: "Hail, Master Librarians."
paragraphs.tone: Morgan speaks like a queen in an old story. Jack and Annie answer in a playful way.

paragraphs.context: They grabbed the rope ladder and started up.
paragraphs.simple: They climb up the rope ladder. Inside, Morgan is holding a book and a piece of paper.

paragraphs.context: “I have an important mission for you,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan has a job for them.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says she has an important job for them and asks if they are ready.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s heart pounded. Ever since Morgan had made them Master Librarians
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack has waited a long time for this mission.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's heart beat fast. Since Morgan made them Master Librarians, he had wanted their first mission very much.

paragraphs.context: “You know I collect books for Camelot’s library?” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan reminds them that she collects books for the library in Camelot.

background.note: Camelot is the castle of King Arthur in old British stories. In this series, Morgan keeps a library there.

paragraphs.context: “Well, there have been many great libraries lost in history,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many great libraries and stories were lost long ago.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says that in history many great libraries were lost, and many wonderful stories were lost with them.

paragraphs.context: “It is,” said Morgan. “But luckily, with the help of the tree house
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie can help save lost stories.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says that with the tree house and the two Master Librarians, some lost stories can be saved.

paragraphs.context: Morgan showed them the piece of paper.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan shows them a paper with strange writing on it.

paragraphs.context: Morgan smiled. “In a way,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The paper shows the title of a lost story in Latin.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says it is a kind of code. It is really the title of a lost story, written in Latin, the language of the ancient Romans of Italy.

background.note: Latin was the language of ancient Rome. Many English words come from Latin.

paragraphs.context: “Ancient Romans?” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is excited, because he loves everything about the ancient Romans.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said Morgan. “This story was in a library in a Roman town.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They must get the story before the library is lost.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says the story was in a library in a Roman town. Jack and Annie must get it before the library is lost forever.

paragraphs.context: “Good. Do not lose them.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan tells them not to lose their cards. The right people will understand them. She also gives them a book to help, as she always does.

paragraphs.context: Morgan handed Jack a book called Life in Roman Times.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan gives them a research book.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan gave Jack a book about life in Roman times. On the cover there was a Roman town with people in tunics and sandals.

paragraphs.context: “And take this—the name of the story I need,”
paragraphs.simple: Morgan gives Jack the paper with the name of the story. He puts it in his backpack.

paragraphs.context: “Remember,” said Morgan. “Your research book will guide you.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says the book will help them. But in their most dangerous moment, only the old story can save them. First they must find it.
paragraphs.tone: This advice is important. Remember it for later in the story.

paragraphs.context: “Go now,” Morgan said softly.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan tells them to go and not to forget what she told them.

paragraphs.context: “Thanks,” said Jack. He pointed at the cover of the book on Roman times.
paragraphs.simple: Jack points at the book about Roman times and wishes to go there.

paragraphs.context: “I almost forgot—I’m going to help you blend in!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan will help them look like Roman kids.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan shouts over the wind that she will help them look like the people there, so nobody notices them.

paragraphs.context: Before Morgan could answer, the tree house started to spin.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house starts to turn before Morgan can answer.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. He pushed his glasses into place.
paragraphs.simple: Jack opens his eyes and pushes his glasses up.

paragraphs.context: Morgan was gone. And so were Jack’s jeans
paragraphs.simple: Morgan is not there. Jack's jeans, T-shirt, sneakers and backpack are gone too.

paragraphs.context: Instead, he had on a white tunic with a belt
paragraphs.simple: Now Jack was wearing a white tunic with a belt, sandals tied with strings, and a leather bag.

paragraphs.context: He looked at Annie. She was dressed the same way.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wears the same clothes. Morgan made them look like children in an ancient Roman town.

paragraphs.context: “I guess this is what Morgan meant,” said Jack,
paragraphs.simple: Jack understands: this is how Morgan helps them look like the people there.

paragraphs.context: “I feel like Cinderella,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she feels like Cinderella, because magic changed her clothes. She likes them.

background.note: Cinderella is a girl in a fairy tale. Magic changes her old clothes into a beautiful dress.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah,” said Jack, although he felt a little as if he was wearing a dress.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is not so happy with his tunic.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says "yeah", but he thinks the tunic feels a bit like a dress.
paragraphs.tone: A small joke: Jack feels a little silly in his tunic.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked with her. They had landed in a grove of trees.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see a mountain and a town.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house was in a group of trees. On one side there was a calm mountain. On the other side there was a town shining in the sun.

paragraphs.context: “I wonder where we are,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders where they are, so he opens the book about Roman times and reads.

paragraphs.context: Almost 2,000 years ago, on August 24, A.D. 79
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about Pompeii and Mount Vesuvius.
paragraphs.simple: The book says that almost 2,000 years ago Pompeii was a normal Roman town by the sea. Many Romans had holiday homes there, with olive trees on the sides of Mount Vesuvius.

background.note: A.D. 79 is the year 79. "A.D." is used for years after the birth of Jesus Christ.
Mount Vesuvius is a volcano in the south of Italy, near the city of Naples. It is still active today.

paragraphs.context: “It does look like a nice place to go on vacation,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says Pompeii really looks like a nice place for a holiday.

paragraphs.context: He looked in the opposite direction.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looks the other way and sees the mountain. It must be Mount Vesuvius, the volcano.

background.note: Mount Vesuvius is a volcano near the city of Naples in Italy. It is still active today; its last big eruption was in 1944.

paragraphs.context: Annie shivered. “That name sounds scary,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie feels afraid of the mountain.
paragraphs.simple: Annie shook a little. She says the name of the mountain seems scary.

paragraphs.context: “Hey! Did you feel that?” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie feels the ground move a little. It is a small earthquake, a sign that the volcano will erupt.

paragraphs.context: “The ground shook. I heard it rumble, too,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the ground moved and made a low noise. Jack thinks she is just dreaming.

paragraphs.context: Jack frowned. “I think you were just dreaming again,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks Annie is imagining things again.

paragraphs.context: “No, I wasn’t,” said Annie. “Something feels wrong about this place.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she was not dreaming. She feels something is wrong here and wants to go home.

paragraphs.context: “Are you nuts?” said Jack. “We have to find that lost story for Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says Annie is crazy. They must find the story for Morgan, and he has always wanted to see a Roman town.

paragraphs.context: He threw his notebook and the Roman book into his leather bag.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts his books in his leather bag and goes down the rope ladder.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t be chicken,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says it will be fun.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie not to be afraid. He says it will be fun.

paragraphs.context: What’s wrong with her? Jack wondered. Usually I’m the worried one.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is surprised that Annie is afraid.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders why Annie is so worried. Usually Jack is the one who worries.
paragraphs.tone: Funny: this time Jack and Annie have changed places.

paragraphs.context: “Come on,” he pleaded. “We can’t let Morgan down.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks Annie again. They cannot make Morgan sad by not doing the job.

paragraphs.context: Annie let out a big sigh. “Okay, but we’d better find that story fast,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie sighed and said OK, but they must find the story quickly. Then she climbed down.

paragraphs.context: The sun was bright and hot as they took off between the olive trees.
paragraphs.simple: In the hot sun they walk between the olive trees. The volcano is behind them.

background.note: Olive trees grow well in hot, dry places around the Mediterranean Sea. The Romans used olive oil for food, lamps and washing.

paragraphs.context: “That’s weird,” said Annie. “I don’t hear any birds.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie notices that there are no birds singing. The grove is strangely quiet.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry about it,” said Jack. “Maybe they’re all at the beach.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says not to worry; maybe the birds went to the beach. He wants to cross the bridge.
paragraphs.tone: Jack jokes because he does not want to worry.

paragraphs.context: He led the way to a small wooden bridge that crossed a narrow stream.
paragraphs.simple: Jack walked first to a small bridge over a little river. But the river was dry.
paragraphs.tone: No birds and a dry stream: these are signs that something bad will happen.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry,” said Jack. “It just means there hasn’t been much rain.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the stream is dry only because it has not rained much.

paragraphs.context: They crossed the bridge and stepped onto a busy street.
paragraphs.simple: They cross the bridge and walk onto a busy street made of stone.

background.note: Roman streets were made of big flat stones. They had high stepping stones so people could cross without walking in water and dirt.

paragraphs.context: People were buying things in the open shops that lined the street.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The street is busy with shoppers.
paragraphs.simple: There were shops all along the street. Some people hurried and some walked slowly. Kids walked with their parents, and teenagers talked and laughed.

paragraphs.context: They don’t seem very different from people shopping in Frog Creek
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks the Romans are like people at home.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks these people are like shoppers in his town. Only the clothes are different.

paragraphs.context: “How will we ever find the ancient lost library?”
paragraphs.simple: Annie wonders how they can find the library. Jack says to keep watching carefully.

paragraphs.context: They walked past shops that had huge jars in them.
paragraphs.simple: In the shops there were big jars of grain, dried fruit and olives. Meat hung from the ceilings.

paragraphs.context: They passed a noisy tavern where people were eating and drinking.
paragraphs.simple: They passed a loud place where people ate and drank. A young man played music on an instrument with strings.

paragraphs.context: “See, there’s nothing to worry about,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says there is nothing to worry about. The town is not very different from their own time.

paragraphs.context: “See, there’s a barbershop and a shoe shop,” said Jack, pointing.
paragraphs.simple: Jack points to a barber and a shoe shop, just like at home.

paragraphs.context: A boy was getting his hair cut by the barber.
paragraphs.simple: A barber was cutting a boy's hair. A girl and her mother were trying on new sandals.

paragraphs.context: They kept walking, until they passed a bakery
paragraphs.simple: They walk past a bakery with fresh flat bread.

background.note: Archaeologists found round loaves of bread in a Pompeii bakery oven. The bread had turned to charcoal in the eruption.

paragraphs.context: “That bread is like pizza,” said Annie, smiling.
paragraphs.simple: Annie smiles: the flat bread looks like pizza.

paragraphs.context: The good smells from the bakery made him feel even more at home.
paragraphs.simple: The nice smell of bread made Jack feel even more relaxed, as if he was at home. Annie was still smiling.

paragraphs.context: Soon they came to a large square filled with people
paragraphs.mainIdea: They come to the big town square.
paragraphs.simple: They came to a big open place full of people, carts, horses and market stalls.

paragraphs.context: Farmers were selling grapes, garlic, and onions.
paragraphs.mainIdea: People sell food and give talks.
paragraphs.simple: Farmers sold fruit and vegetables. Fishermen sold fish. Some people stood on boxes and talked to small groups.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, I bet this is the forum!” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks this square is the forum. He finds a picture of it in his book.

paragraphs.context: The center of a Roman town was called a forum.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains what a forum is.
paragraphs.simple: The middle of a Roman town was called a forum. People met there to buy and sell things and talk about how the town was run.

background.note: The forum was the main square of a Roman town, with the most important buildings around it.

paragraphs.context: “Jack,” whispered Annie. “Jack!” She tugged on his tunic.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pulls Jack's tunic to make him look.

paragraphs.context: Jack glanced up. Annie nodded toward an old woman
paragraphs.simple: An old woman is looking straight at them.

paragraphs.context: She wore a black cloak. Her gray hair was tangled and wild.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A strange old woman watches them.
paragraphs.simple: The old woman wore a black coat with no sleeves. Her gray hair was messy and she had almost no teeth.

paragraphs.context: The woman pointed a bony finger at Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The old woman points her thin finger at them.

paragraphs.context: “The end is near!” she said in a raspy voice. “Go home, strangers!”
paragraphs.simple: In a rough voice the old woman says that something terrible will happen soon. She tells them to go home.

paragraphs.context: “We’d better get away from her,” said Jack,
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to leave before people start to ask who they are.

paragraphs.context: He put away his notebook. Then he and Annie hurried away.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They hurry away from the woman.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put his notebook away, and they hurried off. The old woman laughed in a high, unkind way behind them.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie hid behind a fruit stall.
paragraphs.simple: They hid behind a fruit stall. After a moment, they looked carefully around the corner.

paragraphs.context: “I don’t know. But she looked nuts to me,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the woman looked crazy to him.

paragraphs.context: Jack sighed and pulled out the book again.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looks in the book and, to his surprise, finds a picture of the old woman.

paragraphs.context: In Roman times, there were people who could see into the future
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains what a soothsayer is.
paragraphs.simple: The book says that in Roman times some people could see what would happen in the future and warn others. They were called soothsayers.

paragraphs.context: “See? She wasn’t nuts,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the woman was not crazy. She was warning them, like Annie's bad dream.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t pay attention to that stuff,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not believe in soothsayers.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie not to listen to the soothsayer. He says people in our time do not believe in soothsayers.

paragraphs.context: “Well, I do,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is sure something bad will happen soon.

paragraphs.context: Jack sighed. “Come on, we have to keep going.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to finish the job.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they must find the library and then leave quickly.

paragraphs.context: They left the fruit stand and kept walking through the forum.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see a big, busy building.
paragraphs.simple: They kept walking. Soon they saw a large building with crowds going in and coming out.

paragraphs.context: Most people in Pompeii did not have a bathtub at home
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains the Public Baths.
paragraphs.simple: Most people had no bathtub at home, so they went to the Public Baths every day. There they washed, swam, played sports and met friends.

background.note: The Public Baths were big buildings with hot and cold pools. For Romans they were like a swimming pool, a gym and a meeting place.

paragraphs.context: They kept walking, until soon they came to a fancy building with large columns.
paragraphs.simple: They come to a beautiful building with big columns.

paragraphs.context: The people of Pompeii believed that many gods and goddesses ruled the world.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains the Temple of Jupiter.
paragraphs.simple: The people of Pompeii believed in many gods. Jupiter was the most important. In his temple they prayed and gave him gifts. Today we call these stories myths.

background.note: The Temple of Jupiter stood at one end of the forum in Pompeii. Jupiter was the king of the Roman gods.

paragraphs.context: “My teacher read myths to us,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie know some myths.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers myths about Hercules and Apollo from school.

background.note: Hercules was a very strong hero in Greek and Roman myths. Apollo was the god of the sun and music.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, my teacher read them, too,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says her teacher read myths too. She likes the stories about Venus and Medusa.

background.note: Venus was the Roman goddess of love. Medusa was a monster in Greek myths with snakes for hair.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, maybe the story we’re looking for is a myth,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Maybe the story is a myth.
paragraphs.simple: Jack guesses that their story might be a myth, an old story about gods and heroes.

paragraphs.context: They left the forum and turned onto a wide street.
paragraphs.simple: They went into a wide street. Jack breathed in quickly in surprise. He saw something hard to believe.

paragraphs.context: Tall warriors with huge muscles were walking in a line.
paragraphs.simple: Tall, very strong fighters walked in a line. They had beautiful helmets and heavy shields.

paragraphs.context: Then he saw that the warriors’ feet were chained together
paragraphs.simple: Jack saw that the fighters' feet were tied together with chains, and guards walked with them.

paragraphs.context: Gladiators were slaves or criminals who fought in the amphitheater
paragraphs.simple: Gladiators were slaves or criminals. They had to fight each other or wild animals in a big round building. The people of Pompeii enjoyed watching these fights.

background.note: The amphitheater in Pompeii was a huge round open building with seats for about 20,000 people.

paragraphs.context: “That’s not fun!” said Annie. “No wonder I think it’s weird here.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says fights like that are not fun. It is not surprising that this place feels strange to her.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie watched as the guards led the gladiators away.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The gladiators go to the amphitheater.
paragraphs.simple: The guards took the gladiators to a building that looked like an open-air sports ground.

paragraphs.context: “That must be the amphitheater,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks the round building is the amphitheater and wants to look.

background.note: A Roman amphitheater was a big, round open building with seats all around. Gladiators fought there. The one in Pompeii is the oldest stone amphitheater we know of.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie started up the street toward the amphitheater.
paragraphs.simple: Many people were near the entrance. They shouted happily as the gladiators walked in.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie started to follow them, but a guard held up his spear.
paragraphs.simple: A guard held up his spear and stopped them. He said children could not go in.

paragraphs.context: “No children allowed,” he said stiffly.
paragraphs.simple: The guard says no children can go in, and tells them to go away.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, run along! Run for your lives!” came a raspy, hissing voice.
paragraphs.simple: A rough voice told them to run away to save their lives. It was the old woman again.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie whirled around. It was the soothsayer.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They turn and see the soothsayer.
paragraphs.simple: They turned around very fast. The soothsayer was waving her thin finger at them.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, no! Her again!” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees the old woman again and wants to leave quickly.

paragraphs.context: But before he could stop her, Annie ran up to the soothsayer.
paragraphs.simple: Annie runs to the soothsayer before Jack can stop her.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, brother,” said Jack. He sighed and went over to Annie
paragraphs.simple: Jack sighs and walks over to Annie and the soothsayer.

paragraphs.context: “All the streams of Pompeii have dried up,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The soothsayer tells about strange signs.
paragraphs.simple: The soothsayer says that all the small rivers in Pompeii have no water now.

paragraphs.context: “All the birds have flown away,” the soothsayer said.
paragraphs.simple: The soothsayer says all the birds have flown away. This is another warning sign.

paragraphs.context: “She said that all the rats left, too,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the rats have left and the cows make strange noises.
paragraphs.tone: Animals often act strangely before a volcano erupts or an earthquake happens.

paragraphs.context: “The sea is boiling hot,” the old woman said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sea and ground are strange too.
paragraphs.simple: The old woman says the sea is very hot and the ground shakes and makes sounds.

paragraphs.context: “Because the end is near,” she whispered hoarsely.
paragraphs.simple: She says, in a rough voice, that the end is coming soon.

paragraphs.context: Jack took the piece of paper from his bag.
paragraphs.simple: Jack shows the Latin title to the soothsayer and says the book is in a library in this town.

paragraphs.context: The soothsayer stared for a moment at the card
paragraphs.mainIdea: The soothsayer understands who they are.
paragraphs.simple: The soothsayer looked at the shiny letters on the library card. Then she smiled kindly at them.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, I understand now,” she said. “The only library I know is in the house of Brutus.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: She tells them where the library is.
paragraphs.simple: She says the only library she knows is in the house of Brutus, a big villa at the end of the street.

paragraphs.context: “Brutus and his household are all in Rome,”
paragraphs.simple: The soothsayer says Brutus and his family are in Rome. The villa is only their holiday house.

background.note: Rome was the capital of the Roman Empire. Today it is the capital of Italy.

paragraphs.context: “But we can’t just go in and take something of theirs,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they cannot just walk into someone's house and take their things.

paragraphs.context: The old woman shook her head sadly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: She says nothing will be left.
paragraphs.simple: The old woman shook her head. She says that after today there will be nothing left in Pompeii.

paragraphs.context: Then Annie and Jack started running to the vacation villa.
paragraphs.simple: They run to the holiday house as fast as they can.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran up to the front entrance of the villa.
paragraphs.simple: They run to the front door of the villa, and Jack pushes it open.

background.note: A Roman villa was a large, rich house, often in the country or by the sea. Rich Romans had villas for holidays.

paragraphs.context: The main hall had a large opening in the ceiling.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The hall has a hole in the roof and a pool.
paragraphs.simple: There was a big hole in the ceiling of the hall. Under it was a small stone pool with water in it.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, I bet rain comes through the hole,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack guesses what the pool is for.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks rain comes in through the hole and falls into the pool, so the family can use the water.

background.note: Jack is right. A Roman house had a hole in the roof of the main hall, and a pool below to catch rain water.

paragraphs.context: “Okay, okay, calm down,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie to calm down, puts away his notebook and follows her.

paragraphs.context: Jack trailed behind her. Even though she had already checked the rooms
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to see the Roman house.
paragraphs.simple: Jack walked slowly behind Annie and looked into each room, because he wanted to see a Roman house.

paragraphs.context: The first two rooms had wooden beds.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rooms have beds and pictures.
paragraphs.simple: The first rooms had wooden beds, painted walls and floors made of tiny colored stones.

background.note: Romans made pictures on floors with very small pieces of colored stone. This is called a mosaic.

paragraphs.context: The third room had a low table with silver dishes on it.
paragraphs.simple: The third room had a low table with silver plates and three couches with pillows around it.

paragraphs.context: “This must be the dining room,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says rich Romans lay on couches while they ate.

paragraphs.context: Jack followed her voice. She was in a garden off the dining room.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was in a garden next to the dining room. It had a stone floor, palm trees, grape plants and a pond with a mermaid fountain and goldfish.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked with her. Along the walls of the room were long shelves
paragraphs.mainIdea: The room has rolls of paper.
paragraphs.simple: In the room there were long shelves full of rolls of paper.

paragraphs.context: He pulled out his book on Roman times.
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds a part about writing in his book.

paragraphs.context: Romans used pens made of small reeds.
paragraphs.simple: Romans wrote with pens made from plants. Their ink was partly made from octopus ink. Their "books" were long rolls of papyrus paper.

background.note: Papyrus is a tall water plant from Egypt. People pressed it flat to make a kind of paper.

paragraphs.context: “Aha!” said Jack. “That’s a library of scrolls!
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the room with rolls is a library of scrolls. Their story must be there!

paragraphs.context: Jack threw open the door to the room of scrolls.
paragraphs.simple: Jack opens the door, and they run to the shelves.

paragraphs.context: They began frantically unrolling scrolls one by one.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They look at the scrolls very fast.
paragraphs.simple: They opened the scrolls one after another, very quickly. All of them were written by hand in Latin.

paragraphs.context: She held up a scroll. The words at the top matched
paragraphs.simple: Annie holds up a scroll with the same words as their paper.

paragraphs.context: Annie handed the scroll to Jack, then started out of the room.
paragraphs.simple: Annie gives the scroll to Jack and starts to leave.

paragraphs.context: He put the scroll in the leather bag.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack finds a picture of the volcano.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put the scroll in his bag and looked through the book. In the middle he found a picture of a volcano erupting over a town.

paragraphs.context: For 800 years, Mount Vesuvius was a peaceful mountain
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells when the volcano erupted.
paragraphs.simple: For 800 years the mountain was quiet. Then at noon on August 24, A.D. 79, it became a deadly volcano.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, no,” whispered Jack. “August 24, A.D. 79—that’s today!
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees that today is the day of the eruption. He wants to know the time. But Annie is gone again.

paragraphs.context: Jack grabbed the leather bag. Then, clutching the book
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack runs out of the room.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took the bag and, holding the book tightly, ran very fast out of the scroll room.

paragraphs.context: “So that’s what the soothsayer meant!” Annie said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie understands the warning now: the end is near.

paragraphs.context: “A sundial!” he said. “That’s how the Romans told time!”
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees a sundial. He knows the Romans used sundials to find out the time.

background.note: A sundial is a clock that uses the sun. A stick makes a shadow, and the shadow points to the time.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie raced to the sundial.
paragraphs.simple: They run to the sundial to find out the time.

background.note: A sundial tells the time with the shadow of the sun. Romans had sundials in gardens and public places.

paragraphs.context: His hands shook as he turned the pages of the book.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack compares the pictures with the sundial.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's hands shook. He found a picture of a sundial with different times and looked from the book to the real sundial again and again.

paragraphs.context: The shadow on the sundial can hardly be seen at noon.
paragraphs.mainIdea: At noon there is almost no shadow.
paragraphs.simple: At twelve o'clock the sun is high, so the shadow is very small. That means it is noon now.

paragraphs.context: Just then he heard a terrible blast.
paragraphs.simple: At that moment there was a terrible, very loud sound, the loudest Jack had ever heard.

paragraphs.context: The next thing Jack knew, he was lying on the stone patio.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack finds himself on the ground.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly Jack was lying on the stone floor of the garden. The stones were shaking, and a low noise came from the ground.

paragraphs.context: Everything was shaking and crashing down around them
paragraphs.simple: Pots, plants and the fountain shook and fell. Water from the pond splashed onto the patio and onto Jack and Annie.

paragraphs.context: They both jumped up just as roof tiles began falling into the garden.
paragraphs.simple: They jump up as tiles fall from the roof.

paragraphs.context: Giant cracks split the stone floor
paragraphs.simple: Big lines broke open in the stone floor as they ran to a window.

paragraphs.context: Glowing rocks were bursting through the sky above Mount Vesuvius.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The top of the mountain is gone.
paragraphs.simple: Bright, hot rocks flew up into the sky. The whole top of the mountain had blown away.

paragraphs.context: When a volcano erupts, hot melted rock called “magma”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains magma and lava.
paragraphs.simple: When a volcano erupts, hot melted rock comes up from inside the earth. Inside, it is called magma. Outside, it is called lava.

paragraphs.context: “Lava! That’s like burning mud!” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack explains that lava is like burning mud.

paragraphs.context: There was no running lava from Mount Vesuvius.
paragraphs.simple: Mount Vesuvius did not have running lava. The magma cooled so fast that it became small gray-white rocks called pumice. Pumice is light and has holes like a sponge.

paragraphs.context: A great cloud of pumice, ash, and burning rock shot miles into the air.
paragraphs.simple: A huge cloud of pumice, ash and burning rock went very high into the air. When it fell on Pompeii, it covered the whole town.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out again. A thick black cloud was spreading over the earth
paragraphs.simple: A thick black cloud covered the sky like an umbrella. The sun disappeared and the sky became smoky gray.

paragraphs.context: Just then the ground trembled again.
paragraphs.simple: The ground shook again. Pieces of the ceiling fell on the scrolls.

paragraphs.context: They ran from the scroll library into the garden. Ash and pumice began to fall.
paragraphs.simple: They run into the garden. Ash and light stones begin to fall from the sky.

paragraphs.context: They hurried to the couches beside the table and each grabbed a pillow.
paragraphs.simple: They each take a pillow from the couches by the table to protect their heads.

background.note: Rich Romans ate their dinner lying on couches around a low table.

paragraphs.context: They both pulled off the belts from around their tunics.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They tie pillows on their heads.
paragraphs.simple: They took off their belts and used them to tie the pillows on their heads, like big hats.
paragraphs.tone: A clever idea in a terrible moment: the pillows protect their heads from falling rocks.

paragraphs.context: They stepped over pieces of fallen roof tiles and ran into the main hall.
paragraphs.simple: They step over broken tiles, run into the hall and push open the front door.

paragraphs.context: A blast of heat and dust nearly knocked them over.
paragraphs.simple: Hot air and dust almost made them fall. Outside, small rocks fell on their pillow hats like rain.

paragraphs.context: The hot, dusty air smelled like rotten eggs
paragraphs.simple: The air was hot and smelled very bad. In the forum, all the people were running in all directions.

paragraphs.context: Jack followed her as they ran past the Temple of Jupiter.
paragraphs.simple: They ran past the temple. Its big columns had fallen, and its walls were breaking into pieces.

paragraphs.context: They ran past the Public Baths just as its roof caved in.
paragraphs.simple: As they run past the Public Baths, the roof falls in.

paragraphs.context: “The olive grove and the bridge are near the street with all those open shops!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers that the grove and the bridge are near the street with the shops.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up at the erupting mountain.
paragraphs.simple: A red-hot cloud rose over the mountain. Jack remembers that the mountain was behind them when they came, so they must go toward it.

paragraphs.context: So while others ran away from Mount Vesuvius, Jack and Annie ran toward it.
paragraphs.simple: Everyone else ran away from the volcano, but Jack and Annie ran toward it, because the tree house was there.
paragraphs.tone: This is surprising and brave: they run toward the danger.

paragraphs.context: On the street with the open shops, baskets and broken jars rolled
paragraphs.simple: On the shop street, baskets and broken jars roll over the cracked stones.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran past the bakery and the shoe shop.
paragraphs.simple: They passed the shops they saw before. Now they were all empty, because the owners had run away.

paragraphs.context: The closer they got to the volcano, the more the ground trembled.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It gets worse near the volcano.
paragraphs.simple: As they got nearer to the volcano, the ground shook more, and it got darker and more dusty.

paragraphs.context: “Look! The olive grove!” shouted Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees the olive grove. The tree house is close!

paragraphs.context: Jack could hardly see, but he followed Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack almost could not see, but he followed Annie to the dry stream near the olive trees.

paragraphs.context: They looked around wildly. The bridge had vanished.
paragraphs.simple: They look around in fear. The bridge has disappeared.

paragraphs.context: They stared at the dried-up stream.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The stream is full of pumice.
paragraphs.simple: They looked at the dry stream. Pumice had made big piles there, like snow.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie slid down the bank onto the piles of pumice.
paragraphs.simple: They slide down onto the piles of pumice. As they move, more pumice falls.

paragraphs.context: Jack tried to move through the millions of warm, grayish white pebbles.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tried to walk through the warm gray stones, but he could not move. He was stuck.

paragraphs.context: At the moment, Jack couldn’t remember anything.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is too tired to think.
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not remember anything then. He was too tired and could not think clearly.

paragraphs.context: Jack lifted his bag into the air, above the sea of pumice.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie asks the story for help.
paragraphs.simple: Jack held his bag up above the pumice. Annie took out the old scroll and held it up to the sky.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt himself sink deeper and deeper into the pumice.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was going down into the pumice. Then a deep voice said, "Get up, son!"

paragraphs.context: Then someone lifted Jack up into the air.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly someone picks Jack up into the air.

paragraphs.context: A great flash of fire lit the dusty darkness.
paragraphs.simple: In a flash of red light Jack saw the biggest, strongest man he had ever seen. He looked like a gladiator, but even bigger.

paragraphs.context: He held Jack with one hand and Annie with the other.
paragraphs.simple: The huge man holds them both and puts them on the other side of the stream.

paragraphs.context: “Run!” the giant gladiator boomed. “Before it’s too late!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The giant tells them to run.
paragraphs.simple: The giant shouted in a very loud, deep voice: "Run before it is too late!"

paragraphs.context: They jumped over fallen branches.
paragraphs.simple: They jumped over fallen branches and big cracks in the ground and finally came to the tree house.

paragraphs.context: They grabbed the rope ladder and scrambled up to the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: They climb up the rope ladder quickly.

paragraphs.context: “Where’s the Pennsylvania book?” Jack shouted.
paragraphs.simple: Jack shouts for the Pennsylvania book. Ash and dust are in his eyes, so he cannot find it.

background.note: The Pennsylvania book is a book about their home town. When they wish to go there, the tree house takes them home.

paragraphs.context: Absolutely, wonderfully, peacefully still.
paragraphs.simple: Everything stopped moving. It was quiet and calm, and it felt wonderful.
paragraphs.tone: The three long words make the quiet feel slow and peaceful after all the noise.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t move. He had never been so tired in all his life.
paragraphs.simple: Jack lies still. He has never been so tired.

paragraphs.context: Jack gulped in cool, clean air.
paragraphs.simple: Jack quickly took in big breaths of cool, clean air. He opened his eyes but could not see anything.

paragraphs.context: Jack took off his glasses. The first thing he saw was his backpack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack takes off his dirty glasses. Their Roman clothes and bag are gone.

paragraphs.context: Jack let out a long, deep breath.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan is happy they are safe.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed out slowly. While he cleaned his glasses, Morgan said she was glad they were safe and not hurt.

paragraphs.context: Morgan le Fay stood in the corner of the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan is in the corner of the tree house, as beautiful and mysterious as always.

paragraphs.context: “I know. But you were truly brave,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says they were really brave. They saw a famous event in history. Today scientists study what is left of Pompeii.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said Morgan. “But most of the people of Pompeii did escape.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says most people of Pompeii got away. The city was not completely covered with ash until the next day.

paragraphs.context: “We were almost trapped,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Morgan that a huge gladiator helped them when they asked the story for help.

paragraphs.context: Jack reached into his pack. He breathed a sigh of relief.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked in his bag and was very happy: the scroll was still there, covered with dust and ash.

paragraphs.context: “I am deeply grateful,” she said softly.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says she is very thankful. They put themselves in great danger to bring her the story.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry about it,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it was nothing. He does not want Morgan to know how afraid he was.
paragraphs.tone: Jack acts brave, but the reader knows he was very scared.

paragraphs.context: Morgan smiled. “You are amazing Master Librarians,”
paragraphs.simple: Morgan asks if they are ready to save another ancient story.

paragraphs.context: Morgan laughed. “No. Take a nice vacation.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their next trip is to China.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan tells them to enjoy their holiday and come back in two weeks. Then they will go to ancient China.

paragraphs.context: “It’s called The Strongest Man in the World,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says the story is called The Strongest Man in the World. It is a lost story about Hercules.

background.term: The Strongest Man in the World
background.note: This is the meaning of the Latin title "Vir Fortissimus in Mundo".

paragraphs.context: “Yes, he was one of the heroes of the Greeks and the Romans,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hercules was a hero and a son of Jupiter.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says Hercules was a hero for the Greeks and the Romans. He was a son of the god Jupiter.

paragraphs.context: “I’m taking it back now to Camelot’s library,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan will take the story to Camelot.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan will take the scroll to the library in Camelot. Everyone will read it because of them.

background.note: Camelot is King Arthur's castle in the old British stories. Morgan's library is there.

paragraphs.context: As she waved, the wind began to whirl.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan and the tree house leave.
paragraphs.simple: The wind turned round and round, the tree house spun, and Morgan and the tree house were gone in a flash of shadow and light.

paragraphs.context: “We were saved by Hercules!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they asked the story for help, and then Hercules came.

paragraphs.context: “That’s not possible,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it cannot be true. It was just a gladiator. Hercules is from a myth, so he was never a real person.

paragraphs.context: “Hercules is a myth to people in this time,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says that today Hercules is a myth. But in Roman times many people believed he was real. They were in Roman times, so he was real for them too.
paragraphs.tone: Annie's "simple explanation" is a clever way of thinking about magic and history.

paragraphs.context: “Did you ever hear the saying?” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the old saying: "When in Rome, do as the Romans do." When you are in a place, do what the people there do.
hardWords: when in rome do as the romans do

background.term: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
background.note: A famous English saying. Here it is also a joke, because they really were in Roman times.

paragraphs.context: Jack laughed. “Yeah.” He looked up at the sky.
paragraphs.simple: Jack laughs. He looks at the sky and quietly says thank you to Hercules, whatever he really is.

paragraphs.context: “Jack! Annie!” their dad called from their front porch.
paragraphs.simple: Their dad calls them: it is time to leave for their vacation.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, I hope nothing exciting happens on our vacation,”
paragraphs.simple: After this adventure, Annie and Jack both hope their family vacation will be very quiet and boring.
paragraphs.tone: A joke: usually children want an exciting vacation, but they have had enough excitement.

paragraphs.context: 1) Pompeii was forgotten after it was buried in ash and pumice.
paragraphs.simple: People forgot Pompeii. In 1594 workmen found it while digging a tunnel. Later they found Herculaneum too, which was buried by hot mud. Many everyday things were found in both towns, and recently a library of scrolls.

paragraphs.context: 2) The language of the ancient Romans was called Latin.
paragraphs.simple: The Romans spoke Latin. Many English, French and Spanish words come from Latin. For example, "liber" means book in Latin, and English has the word "library".

paragraphs.context: 3) Mount Vesuvius erupted in the year A.D. 79.
paragraphs.simple: A.D. means "anno Domini", Latin for "in the year of the Lord". It counts from the year Jesus Christ was born, about 2,000 years ago.

paragraphs.context: 4) The Romans took their name from the city of Rome
paragraphs.simple: The Romans were named after the city of Rome, the capital of their empire. Today Rome is the capital of Italy.

paragraphs.context: 5) In A.D. 79, the Romans had a powerful army.
paragraphs.simple: In A.D. 79 the Romans had a strong army. They ruled Western Europe, the Near East and North Africa.

paragraphs.context: 6) Hercules is the Roman name for the hero from the Greek myths
paragraphs.simple: In Greek myths the hero is called Heracles. When the Romans took control of Greece, they took many Greek heroes and gods as their own. Heracles became Hercules.

sentences.context: The idea for this Magic Tree House book was inspired by a small article I read in the newspaper.
sentences.simple: I got the idea for this book from a short newspaper story.
sentences.main: The idea was inspired by an article.

parts.text: The idea for this Magic Tree House book
parts.job: Who or what: the thing the sentence is about.
parts.meaning: My idea for this book

parts.text: was inspired by a small article
parts.meaning: came from a short piece of writing
that I read in the newspaper.

sentences.grammar: "Was inspired by" is the passive form: the article gave her the idea. "I read in the newspaper" tells you which article (we can leave out "that").

sentences.context: The same volcano destroyed a nearby town that might sound more familiar to you—Pompeii.
sentences.simple: This volcano also destroyed another town near it. You may know its name: Pompeii.
sentences.main: The volcano destroyed a town.

parts.meaning: This volcano
broke completely a town close by

parts.text: that might sound more familiar to you
parts.meaning: that you maybe know better
— its name is Pompeii.

sentences.grammar: "That might sound more familiar" tells you more about the town. The dash (—) gives the name at the end, to make it stronger.

sentences.context: Even if Morgan sent them on an adventure, they would return at exactly the same time that they left.
sentences.simple: If Morgan sent them on an adventure, they would still come back at the same time they left.
sentences.main: They would return at the same time.

parts.text: Even if Morgan sent them on an adventure,
parts.meaning: If Morgan sent them on a trip, this would still be true:
they would come back

parts.text: at exactly the same time that they left.
parts.meaning: at the very same time they went away.

sentences.grammar: "Even if" means "it does not matter if". "Would return" talks about what will happen if something else happens.

sentences.context: Ever since Morgan had made them Master Librarians, he had been longing for their first mission.
sentences.simple: Since Morgan made them Master Librarians, Jack had wanted their first mission very much.
sentences.main: He had been longing for their first mission.

parts.text: Ever since Morgan had made them Master Librarians,
parts.meaning: From the time Morgan made them Master Librarians,
he had wanted very much
their first important job.

sentences.grammar: "Had been longing" (past perfect continuous) shows a feeling that went on for a long time before this moment.

sentences.context: “But luckily, with the help of the tree house and you two Master Librarians, some of those stories can be saved.
sentences.simple: But it is lucky that the tree house and you two can help, so we can save some of those stories.
sentences.main: Some stories can be saved.

parts.meaning: But it is good luck that

parts.text: with the help of the tree house and you two Master Librarians,
parts.meaning: because the tree house and you two help,

parts.text: some of those stories can be saved.
parts.meaning: we can save some of those stories.

sentences.grammar: "Can be saved" is passive: somebody (Jack and Annie) can save them.

sentences.context: But remember: In your darkest hour, only the ancient story can save you.
sentences.simple: Remember: when things are worst and most dangerous, only the old story can help you.
sentences.main: Only the ancient story can save you.

parts.meaning: But do not forget this:
At the worst, most dangerous time,

parts.text: only the ancient story can save you.
parts.meaning: nothing else can help you, only the old story.

sentences.grammar: "Darkest hour" is not about light. It means the worst time. "Only" makes the story the one and only thing that can help.

sentences.context: They built large houses called villas and planted groves of olive trees along the slopes of a mountain called Mount Vesuvius (vuh-SOO-vee-us).
sentences.simple: They built big houses named villas, and they planted olive trees on the sides of Mount Vesuvius.
sentences.main: They built houses and planted trees.

parts.text: They built large houses called villas
parts.meaning: They made big houses that were named villas

parts.text: and planted groves of olive trees
parts.meaning: and they planted groups of olive trees

parts.text: along the slopes of a mountain
parts.meaning: on the sides of a mountain

parts.job: The name, and how to say it.
parts.meaning: named Mount Vesuvius.

sentences.grammar: One subject ("They") does two things, joined by "and". "Called ..." gives a name. The part in ( ) shows how to say the name.

sentences.context: “How will we ever find the ancient lost library?” said Annie, glancing around.
sentences.simple: Annie looked around quickly and asked how they could find the old library.
sentences.main: Annie said, "How will we find the library?"

parts.text: “How will we ever find the ancient lost library?”
parts.meaning: "How can we find the old, lost library?"
Annie said,

parts.job: What she did at the same time.
parts.meaning: while she looked around quickly.

sentences.grammar: "Ever" in a question makes it stronger: it sounds hard or impossible. The -ing word ("glancing") shows something done at the same time.

sentences.context: The forum was the main place where people met to sell goods and discuss politics.
sentences.simple: People came to the forum to sell things and to talk about how the town was run.
sentences.main: The forum was the main place.

parts.text: The forum was the main place
parts.meaning: The forum was the most important place
where people came together

parts.text: to sell goods and discuss politics.
parts.meaning: to sell things and talk about running the town.

sentences.grammar: "Where people met" tells you more about "the place". "To sell ..." tells you why.

sentences.context: Not only did people wash at the baths, but they also swam, played sports, and visited with their friends.
sentences.simple: At the baths, people washed. They also swam, did sports and talked with friends.
sentences.main: People washed, swam, played sports and visited friends.

parts.text: Not only did people wash at the baths,
parts.meaning: People washed at the baths, and that is not all:

parts.text: but they also swam, played sports, and visited with their friends.
parts.job: Second part: more things they did.
parts.meaning: they also swam, played sports and talked with friends.

sentences.grammar: "Not only ... but also ..." adds more. After "Not only" at the start, the word order changes: "did people wash" (like a question).

sentences.context: Gladiators were slaves or criminals who fought in the amphitheater (AM-fuh- thee-uh-ter).
sentences.simple: Gladiators were slaves or people who broke the law. They had to fight in a big round building.
sentences.main: Gladiators were slaves or criminals.

parts.meaning: Gladiators were people who were owned by others or who broke the law
and they fought in the big round building
(how to say "amphitheater").

sentences.grammar: "Who fought ..." tells you more about the gladiators.

sentences.context: “Yes, run along! Run for your lives!” came a raspy, hissing voice.
sentences.simple: A rough voice that sounded like a snake said: "Go away! Run to save your lives!"
sentences.main: A voice came.

parts.text: “Yes, run along! Run for your lives!”
parts.meaning: "Yes, go away! Run, or you will die!"
a rough voice that sounded like a snake said.

sentences.grammar: The words come first, then "came a ... voice". This order (verb before the subject) is common in stories after something someone says.

sentences.context: “Brutus and his household are all in Rome,” the soothsayer said. “That is merely their vacation villa.”
sentences.simple: The soothsayer said that Brutus and his family were in Rome; this house is only for their holidays.
sentences.main: The soothsayer said Brutus is in Rome.

parts.text: “Brutus and his household are all in Rome,”
parts.meaning: "Brutus and all the people in his house are in Rome,"
the soothsayer said.
"That is only their holiday house."

sentences.grammar: "Merely" means "only, just". It shows the villa is not very important to them.

sentences.context: Jack trailed behind her.
sentences.simple: Jack walked slowly behind Annie.
sentences.main: Jack trailed behind her.

parts.meaning: Jack
walked slowly after her.

sentences.grammar: "Trail behind" = follow slowly, some way back.

sentences.context: Even though she had already checked the rooms, he took a quick peek in each of them.
sentences.simple: Annie had already looked in the rooms, but Jack still looked quickly in each one.
sentences.main: He took a quick peek in each room.

parts.text: Even though she had already checked the rooms,
parts.job: Something that is surprising with the main part.
parts.meaning: Annie had looked in the rooms before, but still
Jack looked quickly
into every room.

sentences.grammar: "Even though" = "although". "Had already checked" (past perfect) happened before Jack looked.

sentences.context: They wrote their “books” on scrolls of papyrus (puh-PI-rus) paper.
sentences.simple: Their "books" were long rolls of papyrus paper.
sentences.main: They wrote their books on scrolls.

parts.meaning: They wrote what they called "books"
on long rolls of paper made from the papyrus plant.

sentences.grammar: The quote marks around "books" show they were not books like ours. They were scrolls.

sentences.context: Then, clutching the book, he tore out of the scroll room.
sentences.simple: Then he ran very fast out of the room, holding the book tightly.
sentences.main: He tore out of the room.

parts.meaning: Then

parts.job: What he did at the same time.
parts.meaning: holding the book very tightly,

parts.text: he tore out of the scroll room.
parts.meaning: he ran very fast out of the scroll room.

sentences.grammar: "Clutching ..." is an -ing part: it happens at the same time. "Tore out of" means ran out very fast.

sentences.context: The next thing Jack knew, he was lying on the stone patio.
sentences.simple: Suddenly Jack was lying on the stone floor of the garden; he did not know how he got there.
sentences.main: He was lying on the patio.

parts.meaning: Suddenly, after a moment Jack did not notice,

parts.text: he was lying on the stone patio.
parts.meaning: he was lying on the stone floor outside.

sentences.grammar: "The next thing (someone) knew" shows that something happened so fast that the person did not notice it.

sentences.context: Everything was shaking and crashing down around them—pots, plants, the mermaid fountain.
sentences.simple: All the things around them were shaking and falling: pots, plants and the fountain.
sentences.main: Everything was shaking and crashing down.

parts.text: Everything was shaking and crashing down
parts.meaning: All things were moving and falling noisily
all around them
— for example, pots, plants and the mermaid fountain.

sentences.grammar: The dash (—) gives a list of examples of "everything".

sentences.context: The magma from the volcano cooled so fast that it froze into small grayish white rocks called pumice (PUM-iss).
sentences.simple: The hot rock cooled very quickly and became small gray-white stones called pumice.
sentences.main: The magma froze into rocks.

parts.meaning: The melted rock from the volcano
got cold very quickly

parts.text: that it froze into small grayish white rocks
parts.meaning: so it became hard, small gray-white rocks
with the name pumice.

sentences.grammar: "So fast that ..." shows a result: it was very fast, and because of this it froze. "Froze" here means became hard, not ice.

sentences.context: A thick black cloud was spreading over the earth like an umbrella.
sentences.simple: A thick black cloud slowly covered the land, like an open umbrella.
sentences.main: A cloud was spreading.

parts.meaning: A thick black cloud
was opening out and covering the land

parts.job: A picture to help you see it.
parts.meaning: in the shape of an umbrella.

sentences.grammar: "Like an umbrella" compares the cloud to something we know (a simile).

sentences.context: So while others ran away from Mount Vesuvius, Jack and Annie ran toward it.
sentences.simple: Other people ran away from the volcano, but Jack and Annie ran to it.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie ran toward it.

parts.text: So while others ran away from Mount Vesuvius,
parts.meaning: So, at the time other people ran away from the volcano,

parts.text: Jack and Annie ran toward it.
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie ran in its direction.

sentences.grammar: "While" here shows a difference between two actions at the same time.

sentences.context: The closer they got to the volcano, the more the ground trembled.
sentences.simple: When they got nearer to the volcano, the ground shook more.
sentences.main: The ground trembled more.

parts.text: The closer they got to the volcano,
parts.meaning: As they came nearer to the volcano,

parts.job: Second part: another thing changes with it.
parts.meaning: the ground shook more and more.

sentences.grammar: "The + -er ..., the more ..." shows that two things change together.

sentences.context: He was too blinded by ash and dust to find the book that always took them home.
sentences.simple: There was so much ash and dust in his eyes that he could not find the book that takes them home.
sentences.main: He was too blinded to find the book.

parts.text: He was too blinded by ash and dust
parts.meaning: Ash and dust made him unable to see,
so he could not find the book
that always brings them home.

sentences.grammar: "Too ... to ..." means so much that you cannot do something.

sentences.context: “Yes,” said Morgan. “But most of the people of Pompeii did escape.
sentences.simple: Morgan said yes, but most people of Pompeii really got away.
sentences.main: Most of the people did escape.

parts.meaning: Morgan said yes.

parts.text: “But most of the people of Pompeii
parts.meaning: But most people in Pompeii
really got away.

sentences.grammar: "Did escape" (not just "escaped") makes the verb stronger. We use "did + verb" to say "really".

sentences.context: “Hercules is a myth to people in this time,” said Annie. “But in Roman times, lots of people believed he was real.
sentences.simple: Annie said that today people think Hercules is only a story, but long ago many people believed he was real.
sentences.main: Hercules is a myth today.

parts.text: “Hercules is a myth to people in this time,”
parts.meaning: "For people today, Hercules is only an old story,"
Annie said.
But long ago in ancient Rome,

parts.text: lots of people believed he was real.
parts.meaning: many people thought he really lived.

sentences.grammar: "But" shows the two ideas are different. "Believed (that) he was real" tells you what they thought.

sentences.context: Then they took off running for home—and a restful vacation.
sentences.simple: Then they ran home fast, and they went on a quiet, calm vacation.
sentences.main: They took off running for home.

parts.text: Then they took off running for home
parts.meaning: Then they started to run fast to their house
— and to a quiet holiday.

sentences.grammar: "Took off running" means started to run fast. The dash adds a small joke: after this adventure they need a calm vacation.
